According to Mark Gurman's latest *Power On* column, Apple is reportedly considering a complete overhaul of its App Store to boost the platform's potential revenue.

Apple's specific plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reported that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and create more recurring revenue," a direction being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Services SVP Eddy Cue.

The overhaul is reportedly one of the reasons veteran employee Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as SVP of Marketing in 2020 and transitioned to the role of Apple Fellow, with responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller is said to have opposed the idea:

There are various ways Apple could improve App Store profit margins. For instance, it could eliminate its manual app review process—a costly procedure whose effectiveness has diminished in the age of agentic coding. However, users may not welcome further automation of reviews, even if it helps reduce costs.

Apple could also raise developers' annual fees, which currently stand at US$99 per year. Given that many small developers already spend US$200 a month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, some might argue Apple still has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers monthly fees based on usage, passing on some infrastructure costs to them.

The final outcome remains unknown, but I personally am very much looking forward to seeing what form these changes ultimately take.
